title: Orphaned Pod Linger and Scheduler Starvation - Postmortem Draft
content:
Summary:

On 2025-11-06 (UTC) we observed a cluster-wide degradation where nodes exhibited sustained memory pressure and kube-scheduler stalled assigning a subset of pending pods. Several older pods entered Evicting/Terminating states but their API objects remained in the API server for extended periods (up to 6+ hours). Customer-facing services experienced request tail latency spikes and periodic 503s when autoscaler attempts to spin up replacements were not scheduled.

This draft documents detection, timeline, root cause analysis, mitigations performed, and a draft runbook for future occurrences. The immediate fix (rolling restart of kubelet + CNI restart on affected nodes) was applied during the incident, and a stable long-term mitigation is proposed below.

Impact:
- Duration: ~2025-11-06 07:13 UTC to 2025-11-06 13:46 UTC (full recovery after rolling node remediation)
- Services: api-gateway and transformer-worker pools experienced increased p99 latency and intermittent 503s for ~4 hours; internal jobs delayed
- User-visible: intermittent failures for ~8% of requests to the API tier in the 4-hour window
- Capacity: cluster reported ~15% fewer schedulable pods due to node cordons and unschedulable pods remaining in Terminating state

Detection and Symptoms:
- Pager alert SRE-CPU-MEM-High fired at 07:09 UTC for multiple nodes in region-us-west-2 (memory > 92%)
- Kube-scheduler metrics showed a sharp increase in 'unschedulable_pods' and 'scheduling_latency_seconds' at 07:11 UTC
- API server audit logs show many repeated eviction requests and finalizer removals for pods that were already in Terminating state
- CNI logs (calico) on affected nodes showed flapping of veth pairs and repeated route reprogramming events that coincide with kubelet crashloops on some nodes

Timeline (high level):
- 07:06 UTC: Autoscaler starts scale-up due to host-level memory pressure in several pools
- 07:09 UTC: Node memory alarms and initial page to SRE rotation
- 07:11 UTC: Scheduler backlog starts growing; multiple pods pending for > 30s
- 07:20 UTC: First manual investigation shows many pods stuck Terminating with finalizers waiting on network teardown; CNI shows errors about 'resource not found' for stale endpoints
- 08:00 UTC: Rolling restart of kube-controller-manager attempted on one control plane; no improvement
- 09:10 UTC: Decision to cordon and drain a small subset of highly-affected nodes; drain operations hang for long periods due to DeletePod calls not completing
- 10:15 UTC: Eviction attempts backed off; we restarted kubelet on 8 nodes and restarted calico-node DaemonSet on those nodes — partial improvement
- 12:40 UTC: Remaining Terminating pods cleared as kubelet reconnected and processed grace-period expirations; scheduling latency returned to baseline by 13:46 UTC

Root cause hypothesis (contributing factors):
1) Memory fragmentation + gradual heap growth in a set of user containers caused kernel-level OOM pressure on nodes and frequent kubelet restarts. Repeated restarts left pods in Terminating state where their deletion depended on network teardown finalizers.
2) Calico v3.25 had a regression under heavy interface churn causing iptables/ipsets updates to stall; CNI deletion callbacks did not complete reliably which left pod network endpoints in a partial state. Pods with network finalizers therefore could not finish termination flows.
3) Kube-scheduler prioritization rules + burst of pending pods lead to 'scheduler starvation': the scheduler spent cycles retrying failed bindings for pods targeted to nodes that were temporarily non-Ready, causing longer queue processing times for other pending pods.
4) Our eviction/ejection hierarchy and controller backoff settings allowed too-long grace periods for stuck Terminating pods (we had high default terminationGracePeriodSeconds on many stateful pods), slowing recovery.

Evidence supporting root cause:
- Node journal logs show kubelet SIGSEGVs and restart loops on multiple nodes, aligning with memory pressure windows
- Calico logs include traceback and 'failed to apply policy' errors coincident with the longest Terminating durations
- Scheduler metrics and logs show increased retries for BindRequests to node X that was NotReady for the duration
- API server audit shows repeated DELETE requests for pods that still include 'kubernetes.io/pod-networks' finalizer entries

Immediate mitigations taken during incident:
- Restarted kubelet and calico-node on the most-impacted nodes to clear stuck local state (applied on 8 nodes first, then 4 more)
- Temporarily lowered terminationGracePeriodSeconds via on-the-fly patch for a specific deployment to accelerate pod clears (manual, high-risk; reverted after recovery)
- Drained and cordoned severely affected nodes to prevent new pods being scheduled there while we remediated
- Adjusted autoscaler cooldown to prevent hammering nodes during recovery window

Permanent fixes / action items (owner and ETA suggested):
- Upgrade Calico to v3.26.x that contains fixes for iptables stalls (owner: infra-networking, ETA: Q1 2026)
- Add kubelet OOM-handling tuning and memory-pressure remediation playbook; investigate kernel and container runtime logs for persistent memory leaks (owner: eng-sre + infra, ETA: 2025-12-10)
- Change default terminationGracePeriodSeconds for stateless deployments to 30s and ensure stateful workloads have explicit, reviewed settings (owner: platform-engineering, ETA: 2025-12-01)
- Introduce a scheduler-side fast-fail policy: after N binding retries against a NotReady node within T seconds, deprioritize that node for that pod class (owner: eng-sre and platform-engineering; design doc linked) (ETA: 2026-01-15)
- Add an automated remediation that force-deletes Terminating pods older than X minutes when node is NotReady AND CNI finalizer is blocking deletion for > Y seconds; must be gated behind audit and strict checks (owner: eng-sre, ETA: 2025-12-20)

Draft runbook (for on-call use) - quick steps:
1) Detection: check metric 'kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Terminating"}' and 'kube_scheduler_scheduling_attempts' for sharp increases. Run: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector=status.phase=Terminating -o wide | grep -v Running
2) Identify stuck pods and finalizers: kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'
3) If finalizer is network-related (calico/cni), inspect node calico logs: kubectl logs ds/calico-node -n calico --tail=500 -l kubernetes.io/hostname=<node>
4) If kubelet is crashlooping on the node: ssh into host (or use node SSH jump) and inspect journalctl -u kubelet -b; consider systemctl restart kubelet after collecting logs
5) If pods remain stuck after kubelet and calico restart for > 10m, escalate to targeted restart of calico-node DaemonSet on that node: kubectl delete pod -n calico <calico-pod> --grace-period=0 --force
6) As last resort for customer-impacting events, use force-delete on pod objects with finalizers disabled only after approval: kubectl patch pod <pod> -n <ns> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' --type=merge; kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <ns> --grace-period=0 --force

Monitoring and alert changes proposed:
- Add new alert 'KubeAPI:PodTerminatingStuck' when count of Terminating pods > 50 for > 10m
- Alert 'CNI:EndpointDeleteErrors' when calico agent reports > 5 delete errors per minute per node
- Track scheduler queue depth per pod-class and alert on sustained growth (> 3x baseline for 5m)

Unresolved questions (needs followup):
- What container images or workloads were contributing most to memory fragmentation? Need allocation profiles from the affected nodes (owner: app-owners; due 2025-11-20)
- Can we safely automate force-delete flow without causing data loss for statefulsets? Need guardrails and owner approvals (owner: platform-engineering + product; due 2025-12-05)
- Are there kernel upgrades that would improve memory fragmentation or OOM behavior on our node images? (owner: infra, due 2025-12-15)

Notes and evidence attachments (collected during incident):
- Node journal excerpts and kubelet stack traces (attached to JIRA SRE-3112)
- Calico daemonset logs showing iptables errors between 07:12-08:05 UTC
- API server audit logs showing repeated delete/evict attempts for the same pod objects

Post-incident follow-ups (short term):
- Owners will present a mitigation plan to the SRE weekly sync on 2025-11-18
- Platform-engineering to run calico upgrade in a staging cluster and run a stress test with rapid create/delete of small networked pods (owner: platform-eng; due 2025-11-30)
- Infra to build a small playbook script for safe (logged) force-deletes with required approvals via Slack command and audit trail (owner: eng-sre; prototype due 2025-11-21)

Appendix: useful commands captured during incident:
- List Terminating pods: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector=status.phase=Terminating -o wide
- Inspect pod finalizers: kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'
- Force remove finalizers (manual approval required): kubectl patch pod <pod> -n <ns> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' --type=merge; kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <ns> --grace-period=0 --force
- Restart calico on node: kubectl delete pod -n calico -l kubernetes.io/hostname=<node> --grace-period=0 --force

This document is a working draft. Please add any missing log excerpts, timestamps, or counter-evidence to the JIRA ticket SRE-3112. After review, we will finalize the postmortem and schedule the remediation tasks in the SRE backlog.
